title: POC integration playbook + latency-slice acceptance with customer scripts
summary: Discovery + POC scoping focused on benchmark harness integration: customer scripts, traffic shaping, streaming vs non-streaming paths, success criteria and timeline. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with a mixed-mode harness and three acceptance slices (latency p50/p95, throughput window, quality checks).
topics: Harness integration approach for customer scripts
transcript:
00:00 Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Maya from Redwood. We got Liam on the call for the technical piece. how's everyone today?
00:07 Priya Nair: Good thanks, excited to dig in, we want to make sure the POC shows Helix can hit our latency and cost targets before we commit.
00:13 Liam O'Connor: Great, thanks Priya. quick agenda: we'll walk through the harness handshake, where your scripts plug in, define acceptance slices (latency/throughput/quality), and finish with timeline and action items.
00:25 Andre Gomez: Sounds good. one constraint right away: everything needs to run in our VPC during the pilot because of PHI-ish telemetry. encryption at rest via our KMS is required.
00:34 Maya Chen: Noted — private deployment mode or dedicated with VPC peering are both feasible. we'll capture the exact network flow in the security checklist.
00:42 Samir Patel: For the benchmark, our scripts are written in our internal harness — node/python mix — they stream tokens to the client SDK today. we'll want to test both streaming and non-streaming to compare tail latency.
00:54 Liam O'Connor: Perfect. quick clarification: by streaming you mean chunked token-by-token responses over a long-lived connection, and non-streaming is request/response where the server returns full generation. same definitions we'll use.
01:06 Priya Nair: Exactly. our product team sees a 200-400ms p50 goal on short prompts and p95 under 600ms for interactive flows. for batch scoring, we care more about throughput and cost.
01:18 Liam O'Connor: OK. we usually split acceptance into three slices: interactive slice (short prompts, streaming enabled), workload slice (batch scoring throughput), and quality slice (nLL/accuracy/regression tests). Each has measurable thresholds.
01:30 Andre Gomez: How do we map our customer scripts into the Redwood harness? we don't want to rewrite them.
01:36 Maya Chen: Our harness supports an adapter pattern. customers can supply a wrapper script that reads from your existing format; we maintain small shim libs for node/python. typical work is ~1-2 dev days for a single engineer to adapt scripts.
01:49 Samir Patel: Hmm that's promising. we have a few custom tokens post-processing steps that inspect KV cache and do a quick rerank — will that be preserved?
01:57 Liam O'Connor: Yep — the harness supports pre/post hooks. We can run your post-processing in the client-side adapter or as a step in the harness. only caveat is if you rely on low-level KV cache introspection that the model runtime doesn't expose, we may need to mock or re-implement those bits.
02:12 Priya Nair: For the test matrix, we want three payload types: short chat turns (~20 tokens), medium generation (~150 tokens), and long-context (~2k tokens) for retrieval-augmented flows. can Redwood handle warmup/kv cache priming in the harness?
02:25 Liam O'Connor: Yes — we have warmup scripts that perform prefix priming and KV warm caches. We'll coordinate the cache warmup window. For 2k contexts we'll simulate sequence transcoders and estimate memory. that will factor into GPU sizing.
02:36 Andre Gomez: On sizing — our traffic profile for production peaks at 350 concurrent interactive sessions, average concurrency 120, and batch jobs process ~500k requests per day. For the POC we want to run synthetic peaks to validate autoscale and latency under stress.
02:52 Maya Chen: Good detail — POC sizing plan: 1) baseline single-node throughput test 2) scaled e2e peak simulation to ~1.5x your expected peak (i.e., 525 concurrent) for a 10-minute window 3) long-duration soak at expected production volume. We'll include both streaming and non-streaming runs.
03:10 Samir Patel: How do we compare costs? we need per-1k token unit economics and an estimate for GPU hours for your runtime vs our current infra.
03:19 Liam O'Connor: We'll produce a cost model: tokens-per-second * time * instance rate; we'll run the same workload on Redwood Dedicated (quantized model profile) and estimate MTP/GPU hours. We'll provide a spreadsheet with breakouts.
03:29 Priya Nair: Success criteria — propose we accept if: p50 < 300ms and p95 < 650ms for interactive short prompts; throughput for batch >= 12k requests/hour with avg latency < 2s; and no quality regressions on core prompt set (we have 120 test prompts).
03:45 Maya Chen: That matches what we normally ship as acceptance slices. We'll add an error-rate threshold (HTTP 5xx < 0.1%) and model-fallback behavior documented.
03:54 Andre Gomez: On network — can the pilot run inside our AWS account? we prefer a private deployment with IAM roles and KMS.
04:02 Liam O'Connor: Yes. For private we install our control plane in your VPC with IAM cross-account role or role-assumed worker nodes. We'll provide a template CloudFormation/Terraform sample.
04:13 Samir Patel: About the streaming instrumentation: our client SDK uses a custom SSE-like stream with backpressure handling. will Redwood's runtime surface per-token timings?
04:22 Liam O'Connor: The harness captures timing breakdowns (request received, model first token, token rate, total completion). We can emit token-level traces to your telemetry (Datadog/Prometheus) or to a CSV for post-analysis.
04:35 Priya Nair: Great. let's talk timeline — we want a POC that fits a 2-week window starting Sep 15. Is that realistic?
04:42 Maya Chen: Yes — high-level plan: week 0 (this week) — integration planning and adapter handoff; week 1 — harness integration, warmup, baseline runs; week 2 — peak/safe window runs and acceptance testing. Final report within 3 business days after completion.
04:58 Andre Gomez: Who owns the adapter and how many Redwood SE hours should we budget?
05:02 Liam O'Connor: Typically the customer owns the adapter code with Redwood SE support: 8-16 hours for initial handshake and a 2-4 hour follow-up. If Helix prefers, Redwood can take on the adapter work as professional services and we'll quote it.
05:14 Samir Patel: We have a compliance review too — can you send SOC2 docs and your network diagram?
05:18 Maya Chen: We'll share SOC2 Type II report and the architecture diagram link in the follow-up. Link: https://redwood.example/docs/poc-security (placeholder, will send secure share).
05:28 Priya Nair: For acceptance, how do we handle quality checks? is it automated?
05:32 Liam O'Connor: We'll run your 120 test prompts through the harness and compute a set of metrics: BLEU/ROUGE where applicable, throughput-latency tradeoffs, and a side-by-side token-level diff for any high divergence. Also can plug in your custom eval script.
05:46 Andre Gomez: One concern: our long-context flow uses local retrieval and we want to ensure the KV cache warm strategy doesn't leak internal IDs. can we sanitize logs?
05:54 Liam O'Connor: Yes, logs can be sanitized client-side. We also support PII redaction hooks in the adapter. For private deployment logs never leave your VPC unless you opt in.
06:06 Priya Nair: On metrics, we want to see p50/p90/p95, token-per-second, tail token times, and per-route cost.
06:12 Maya Chen: We'll expose those in the console and export CSVs. We'll also provide a pre-made dashboard template.
06:19 Samir Patel: Streaming vs non-streaming — do you have guidance when to choose which?
06:23 Liam O'Connor: Short answer: streaming helps perceived latency for interactive chat; it can increase server load because of more connections and requires more robust backpressure handling. Non-streaming is simpler and often lower CPU overhead per-request. For tight p95/throughput constraints, non-streaming sometimes wins. For UX-critical apps streaming is preferred; we can quantify both in the POC.
06:44 Priya Nair: Let's define acceptance test runs: run 3 baseline streaming runs (short/medium/long), 3 non-streaming runs, then two peak burst runs at 1.5x concurrency. Each run should be 10 minutes for peak validation and 1 hour for soak.
06:57 Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. We'll also include cold-start tests for first-token cold latency and tail-percentile under autoscale events.
07:05 Andre Gomez: Do we have to modify our auth flows for the harness?
07:08 Maya Chen: No, the harness supports token-based auth and can be configured to use your OAuth/SSO in the VPC path. We'll document the minimal changes.
07:15 Priya Nair: Any competitor comparisons we should run in the POC? we currently test on our on-prem cluster and occasionally on <redacted> cloud endpoints.
07:23 Maya Chen: We can optionally run a comparison against Anthropic/OpenAI/our current infra if you provide credentials and it's within scope. Cost/time considerations apply.
07:31 Samir Patel: Ok. Next steps and action owners?
07:34 Maya Chen: I'll recap and we'll log action items.
07:36 Maya Chen: Action: Send SOC2 docs + private deployment diagram (Owner: Maya) due 2026-09-03.
07:44 Priya Nair: Action: Provide sample of customer scripts and the 120 test prompts (Owner: Priya) due 2026-09-04.
07:51 Andre Gomez: Action: Provision an IaC stub in our AWS account and share cross-account role details (Owner: Andre) due 2026-09-07.
07:59 Liam O'Connor: Action: Prepare harness adapter template and initial shim + estimate SE hours (Owner: Liam) due 2026-09-03.
08:06 Samir Patel: Action: Sanitize and share any PII-sensitive example logs (Owner: Samir) due 2026-09-04.
08:12 Maya Chen: Recap: target start Sep 15, 2-week window, acceptance slices as discussed, we will share a POC runbook and the spreadsheet cost estimates.
08:22 Priya Nair: Sounds good. thanks everyone.
08:24 Andre Gomez: Thanks.
08:26 Liam O'Connor: Bye all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the kickoff.
